 St. Paul homeowner says he is still waiting for his property tax refund
 Richard Reeve KSTP 
 --> 
 St. Paul resident says waiting for his property tax refund has cost him thousands
 A St. Paul homeowner says he is still waiting for a property tax refund he counts on to help pay a large tax bill.
 Steve Jones said he paid his property taxes by Oct. 15 out of pocket while he waited for the refund. 
 He told 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS the money usually arrives earlier and helps cover the second half of his taxes.
 “It’s normally arrives around the end of September, early October and it helps to pay the second half property taxes and this year it didn’t come,” Jones said.
 He said he bought his St. Paul house in 1986 and paid it off by 2006. 
 He added that his 4,000-square-foot home in the city’s Highland neighborhood no longer has a mortgage, so he doesn’t have an escrow account to cover taxes.
 Why the delay?
 Jones said his property tax bill is about $6,400 a year and his refund is about half that. 
 He contacted 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS to ask why the refund had not arrived.
 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS emailed the Department of Revenue asking why refunds were delayed and how many taxpayers were affected.
 Jones said he believed a one-time 15% increase in refunds may have slowed the process, but the Department of Revenue spokesperson said the increase doesn’t impact processing times.
 “The one-time increase itself does not impact processing times for an individual’s return,” a Department of Revenue spokesperson said. “To date, we’ve processed over 507,000 returns, accounting for 88% of returns received, which is ahead of pace compared to prior years.”
 In a statement, the spokesperson said some reviews take longer than others. 
 The statement said some returns need manual review for accuracy, possible fraud, or amendments and that when a refund goes out depends on when a return is filed.
 When refunds go out
 The department also said most homeowner refunds typically go out in September and into October.
 It said the one-time 15% increase this year was manually adjusted for returns filed before mid-July.
 Jones said he did reach someone at the Department of Revenue, who told him his refund would be escalated and that he could get it in about two weeks. 
 He said he is concerned about people who may not be able to afford the October tax payment.
 “For me, we’re fortunate enough now. We’ve got our Social Security, and we are actually old enough to have a few regular pension payments and savings and stuff like that,” Jones said.
 Does he think this could be a hardship for some folks?
 “Of course. I mean, it’s a four-figure number,” Jones said.
